chapter: Young players, schools and studio work
title: Black musicians entering the studios; the Patti Page show
summary: Hinton recalls Ben Webster, Shavers and Cozy Cole breaking in; Maxwell quips about Ernie Royal's section on Patti Page's show.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I can go back even before that, there weren't Jimmy, when/any black musicians in the studios -- and then all of a sudden we've got some powers that be, some friends of the black society, tried to get some black musicians in. And of course they did, eventually, the Ben Websters and the Charlie Shavers and guys of that category, Teddy Wilson, were brought into the studios and when they had shown -- Cozy Cole -- show they could qualify. And these musicians have always been known, black or white, to be the epitome of the musician. You have to be a very flexible man.

Sure. You know, I think jazz musicians would come in, and you would get your friends in. If your friends were black, you would bring them in. I remember I was doing the Patti Page show and asking for a trumpet section, and one time sitting there and Ernie Royal said, what the hell are you doing here? I said, what do you mean, what am I doing here? I got all you guys here.
He said, yeah, but Joe Wilder, Jimmy Nottingham and me, what's a white guy doing in here?
Well, it was cute. So, you know, guys did that and it worked both ways.
Was that the one at CBS?
That's right, I was on that show, too. I (inaudible).
Then we went over to ABC. Now, Clark got me on dates, I got Clark on dates. You know how things were, it goes back and forth.
